games.explanation: Getting plus money on the better team is the whole game, and Detroit is comfortably the better team here regardless of what the pitching matchup suggests on paper. Ashcraft has been sharp against righties but leaks oil against lefties, walking nearly 12% of them, and the Tigers happen to run out a lineup full of left-handed bats who punish exactly that profile. Montero is nobody's ace, but a projected one-run game between a first-division club and a rebuild shouldn't have the rebuild favored on the road. At +131, the market is paying you to take the side with more talent because the name on the mound is unfamiliar.

Cleveland is a favorite here mostly because their uniform says so, not because tonight's matchup actually justifies chalk. Whisenhunt is a walk machine who gets barreled every time hitters make contact, which is the profile that turns a 4-4 game into a 5-4 loss, not a laugher. San Francisco counters with Devers doing his usual damage against righties (a .391 xwOBA that plays anywhere) and a lineup built to punish command-dependent arms. The projected score is basically a coin flip, and getting +175 on a coin flip is how the math tells you the market got lazy.

Wheeler is the best pitcher on the mound by a mile, which is exactly why the price on Miami has drifted into territory it probably shouldn't live in. Coin-flip games happen even when the arms don't match, and our sim has this one landing on the number regardless of the jerseys involved. Gibson isn't going to overpower Schwarber or Harper, but the Marlins get to see Wheeler in a park that plays generously to the pull side, and Marsee and Conine are the kind of right-handed bats capable of turning one mistake into the whole evening. At +212 on a game the model sees closer to a 43% shot, you're getting paid twice for a fight the board has already scored.

Nobody wants to touch the Rockies at Coors as a home dog, which is exactly why the price got this fat. Eric Lauer has been perfectly fine at sea level and a very different pitcher the moment you drop him into thin air with a lineup that actually barrels balls up, and Hunter Goodman is the kind of left-handed power bat that turns his fastball into souvenirs. Feltner isn't inspiring, but his contact profile has been sneakily livable, and a projected six-run game at Coors is a coin flip dressed up as a mismatch. At +173, the board is charging you Dodgers-in-May prices for a Lauer-at-altitude start, and that math doesn't hold up.

Wheeler on the mound usually means the underdog run line is a trap, except the sim keeps spitting out one-run games and the market keeps pricing this like Philly wins going away. Miami's lineup isn't scaring anyone, but Marsee and Conine bring the kind of hard contact that survives an ace, and Gibson has been quietly better than his strikeout rate suggests. The projected score lands at 5.1 apiece, which is not a game you lay a run and a half on either side of. Getting a plus price on the dog plus the hook, in a park that inflates runs and homers, is the whole ticket.

Boston is being priced like the road favorite that always covers, and Ranger Suarez against a righty-heavy Arizona lineup is exactly the profile that lets underdogs hang around into the seventh. Suarez is a lefty who eats left-handed bats alive but plays much closer to average against righties, which is a problem when Perdomo, Carroll, Moreno, and Marte all hit from that side and all carry xwOBAs north of .345 against righties. Merrill Kelly is the flawed arm here on paper, but a park playing down homers and a wind blowing straight in turns this into the kind of grinding four-run affair where a run and a half is a lot of cushion. Getting Arizona plus the run at -140 means you only need the game close, and the shape of this matchup wants it close.

Houston is favored because they're the better team on paper, but a run and a half of cushion changes the entire conversation, and the market hasn't quite caught up to how vulnerable Cristian Javier looks in his return workload. He's walking better than ten percent of the hitters he's faced and giving up hard contact at a rate that suggests the strikeout shine is doing a lot of concealing. Trout gets to see a righty whose stuff hasn't fully returned, Neto has been barreling everything in sight, and the projected margin here is well inside a run. You're getting plus-money-adjacent juice on a game the sim expects to finish within a swing, which is exactly when the run line prints.
